Questions and Answers

1. Revision of the Manual—What it should contain, broad regulation and general instructions versus specific and definite regulations and detailed instructions?

Reply—We favor broad regulations and general instructions in the grazing manual rather than specific and definite regulations and instructions.


2. Range Improvement—POLICY governing construction and needed changes in regulations to accomplish it; how shall cost of maintenance be met; how far should fencing of ranges and small allotments, lambing pastures, ETC., be carried?

Reply—We are opposed to the requirement of existing range improvements constructed by grazing permittees now on the national forest. As to construction of future improvements and maintenance of improvements, local conditions should rule matters in this connection. We believe that this question can be handled satisfactorily only by localities. Concerning the last section of the query, we believe that local conditions also affect this matter, so that it can be decided only by localities.


3. Stock driveways and crossing permits—Should we charge for crossing permits under what circumstances and on what basis? Service policy as to stock driveways in relation to overgrazing and damage to forest reproduction.

Reply—In our opinion, stock driveways across national forests should be provided only where they fit in with the economic needs of the sections concerned. Under such circumstances we do not favor any charges for crossing privileges.


4. Grazing fees—Principles which should govern their establishment and payment; is permanent division of payments desirable?

Reply—As to the grazing fees, we do not believe that under any conditions the establishment of grazing fees on a basis in excess of a rate per head to mean a reasonable cost of grazing administration is warranted.

As to division of grazing payments we believe that a permanent division is desirable, to apply to all classes and periods of permits, and in this connection we suggest July 1st and December 1st as the dates for payment.


5. Annual versus term permits—Why have term permits not been more generally used and satisfactory; advantages and disadvantages of term permits in administration; for what period should they be issued; how should they be modified with view to establishing range use?

Reply—In our judgment, term permits have not been more generally used, because they have not been sufficiently attractive. We consider long term permits as essential to the satisfactory financing, stability and welfare of our business and recommend that these be established for term not less than ten years. Also that there should be no limit restriction as to the numbers for which term permits be granted.


6. Qualifications of applicants—Use and measure of commensurability; qualifications as far as property is concerned; should they depend on ability and commensurability and should not depend on number of stock owned.

Reply—Commensurability standards should be based on the custom and requirement of localities. We believe that dependency should be based on or not the property investment is of such character as to require connection with the range in order to be successfully operated.


7. Preferences—Their value to permittees; should they accrue to the stock or the ranch; should they be transferable as regular assets?

Reply—In our opinion, the economic welfare demands that grazing preferences accrue to the dependent and commensurate property upon which they are based, except where equally dependent and commensurate property is substituted by the parties concerned.


8. Distribution of grazing privileges—Principles that should govern; the small permittee versus the large operator; the new applicants results secured under present policies in stabilizing the use of national forest ranges; should further distribution be restricted, and how?

Reply—In our judgment, grazing privileges should have been and should be distributed to the commensurate and dependent property acquired upon the basis of ability to use the range concerned. We believe the economic welfare depends more upon the principle of connecting the range with the commensurate and dependent property than in connection with distinction between sizes of operations. We do not believe that new interests should be brought into connection with ranges fully occupied by stock owned by interests holding commensurate and dependent property in amount. We believe that it would promote economic welfare to displace privileges not based on fully commensurate and dependent property investment.

Dr. George Lang, personal friend, conducted the funeral services under the great handicap of his own deep feeling. An interesting case of scurvy is being treated in Dawson at the present time interesting because it has occurred in man who has lived in the country and lived we'll for over twenty years. He has been buying very much the same kind of an outfit every fall for years He came to Dawson from his home on the creeks last fall. as usual, and purchased his winters supply of food. This was composed of the fol- lowing articles of diet: Beans, four, rolled oats, crushed wheat. and rice; eggs, butter, bacon, and canned milk: straw berry and apricot jams; dates, raisins and figs. Besides these things he had fresh beef and fresh moose. He lived on this diet for about three months, and found to his surprise that he grew languid; was easily fatigued, and finally became very weak. Ills skin began to show brownish black spots. which developed into purple patches; his appetite failed; his teeth became loose and some came out; hls gums sore and spongY; his joints stiff, and hls arms and legs were swollen and had brawny feel. He thought he was suffering from rheumatism, and came to Dawson for treatment. On consulting physician he was greatly surprised to be told that he had bad case of scurvy.

 It will be noted by referring to the mans diet list that he did not have Do~ tatoes, cranberries, blueberries, rasp- berries or entrants; apples, pears. peaches, plums or apricots, except the jams; lemons. pineapple or lime juice in a word, he did not have any acid fruits. In former years he was able to get the native berries, but last year the summer frosts killed these and he could not put any up for winter, as he had been in the habit of doing, and, therefore, he lived on an improperly balanced ration.

 Since being put on properly bal anced ration by his physician the pa- tient is making rapid recovery.

 Among the foods now being given the patient are a liberal allowance of fresh oranges, lemons, apples, nuts and other foods containing the acids and vitamines which were lacking in the foods he had at home. At the begin hing of the treatment by the physician, raw potatoes and lime juice were given the patient in addition to a good va riety of other foods.

Evans, chief disbursing officer, Department of the Interior, who is retiring on July 1 after fifty-nine years of continuous service to the government in that department, was appointed as a messenger boy in the department by President Lincoln in 1864 and quickly rose to the higher positions until he gained his present office. "I really believe that the old man is right!
When William next comes I will soon let


him know
'Twill be a good chance, by the way, too, to


prove
If he's really sincere in his vows of true


love.
He must give up at once and forever the
wine, For the lips that touch liquor shall never


touch mine!"
She heard a quick step coming over the
moor, And the same merry voice she'd oft heard


before;
Then, ere she could speak, warm arm held
her fast,
And her lover said gently, "I've come, love!
I'm sorry I've kept you long waiting like


this,
But know you'll forgive me—now give me a
kiss!"
But she shook the bright curls on her beau


tiful head
And drew herself up, while quite proudly


she said,

true, For you say that you love me—don't think
you do.

wine,

touch mine!"

clear

dear!"

see

me. I'm jealous, I own, of the poisonous wine,
And the lips that touch liquor shall never
touch mine!"
He then turned quite angry. "Confound it!"


he said.

little head.
But I'll see if I cannot remove it soon


thence!"
She replied, "'Tis not nonsense, but sound
common sense,
And I mean what I say, and this you will


find:
I don't often change when I've made up my


mind!"
He stood all resolute, angry, perplexed;
She never before saw him look half so


vexed.
Still she said, "If he talks all his life I


won't flinch!"
And he talked, but he never could bulge her


inch;
So he cried, with a look of despair and a


groan,
"Oh, Alice, your heart is as hard as a


stone!"
But, though her heart beat in his favor


quite loud,
She still firmly kept to the vow she had


vowed
And at last without even a tear or sigh,
She said, "William, I'm going; so bid you


good-by!"
"Nay, stop!" he then said. "I'll choose one


of the two;
I'll give up the liquor, but cannot lose


you!"
Now, William had ever great cause to re-


joice
From the hour he thus wisely made Alice


his choice;
And he blessed through the whole of life
The decision that gave him his dear little


wife;
And she, by her firmness, won over that


night
A true friend to our cause, and an orna-


ment bright.
Oh, that every fair girl in our drink cursed!

American Falls, Idaho—(A. P.)—

This little agricultural community has consented to plans for its removal to new townsite as the result of negotiations by representatives of the United States government. The present site, according to plans, will be inundated together with 4,000 acres surrounding it, to make way for the construction of the gigantic American Falls reservoir.

Authorization of plans to build the reservoir, which will be the largest in the United States and the fourth largest in the world, with capacity of 100,000 acre-feet of water, was given at recent special election in the American Falls irrigation district. The district embraces approximately 100,000 acres. The cost of the project is estimated at $12,000,000.

Scott, state agricultural statistician, rains have been general over the state, and especially heavy in all the southeast quarter of the state. Harvesting of crops, threshing, and marketing have been delayed, and great damage has resulted to the large bean crop of the southeast. Alfalfa seed, wheat, oats, and other crops have also suffered from the heavy rains. The quality of grains still in the shock has been materially lowered. PARIS, Jan. g, Youth, beauty and grace-these three are the essential qualities of mannequin, declare the fashion designers in Paris who are beseiged daily by women seeking employment.

 Lured by the anticipated pleasure of wearing pretty gowns, women of all classes and of widely-yarying ages are applying to the fashion houses of the Rue de la Paix and the Champs Elysees. Some are no longer in the bloom of youth, others are young enough but very ungain- ly. Many ot them were formerly ill easy circumstances, but have been forced to seek work as a result of the war. Persuading themselves that one needs to be but tall and slender in order to show off handsome gown, they desire to take up the profession" of exhibiting models. All this has raised the question: Can a woman became a mannequin without training?

 "In general" answers Poiret, "the recruiting of a mannequin is some thing like that of a pupil of the Paris Conservatory. About six months of study are necessary-study of the conventional gestures and the art of walking. Youth and beauty are natural gifts, but the ability to pre- sent a frock to the best advantage can only be acquired after months of study of beautiful attitudes, eX- cept in the case of few rare stars who seem born to the trade. The final test nearly always comes With the way she can wear a coat and the tres decollete robe. There are many

 recruits who must be told after few weeks that they will never have beautiful gowns, for they do not know how to wear them

 Many of the would-be models were formerly in society or literary circles and imagine that the only work a mannequin has to do is to show, off lovely robes, forgetting there is a rougher side to the picture, for man. nequins have to spend weary hours trying on" robes when they are being created and retouched. TO many little Parisiennes and country girls the salon of the fashionable dfessmaker exerts the same attrac- ton as the stage. There are lux urious rooms, with soft carpets ana low light and on the big days or the seasons openings there is music and a crowd of chic people. Tales are told of the brilliant marriages or manneuuins, now become important women of society, forgetting to men, tion others who have had lament able end-and their number is legion.

Lured by the anticipated pleasure of wearing pretty gowns, women of all classes and of widely-varying ages are applying to the fashion houses of the Rue de la Paix and the Champs Elysees. Some are no longer in the bloom of youth, others are young enough but very ungainly. Many of them were formerly in easy circumstances, but have been forced to seek work as a result of the war. Persuading themselves that one needs to be but tall and slender in order to show off handsome gowns, they desire to take up the profession of exhibiting models. All this has raised the question: Can a woman become a mannequin without training?

"In general" answers Poiret, "the recruiting of a mannequin is something like that of a pupil of the Paris Conservatory. About six months of study are necessary—study of the conventional gestures and the art of walking. Youth and beauty are natural gifts, but the ability to present a frock to the best advantage can only be acquired after months of study of beautiful attitudes, except in the case of few rare stars who seem born to the trade. The final test nearly always comes with the way she can wear a coat and the tres decollete robe. There are many recruits who must be told after few weeks that they will never wear beautiful gowns, for they do not know how to wear them.

Many of the would-be models were formerly in society or literary circles and imagine that the only work a mannequin has to do is to show off lovely robes, forgetting there is a rougher side to the picture, for mannequins have to spend weary hours trying on robes when they are being created and retouched. To many little Parisiennes and country girls the salon of the fashionable dressmaker exerts the same attraction as the stage. There are luxurious rooms, with soft carpets and low light and on the big days of the seasons openings there is music and a crowd of chic people. Tales are told of the brilliant marriages of mannequins, now become important women of society, forgetting to mention others who have had lamentable end—and their number is legion.

During this time the undergraduates and public in general had the opportunity to hear such men as Professor Alfred J. Pribram of the University of Vienna, Professor William L. Westermann of Cornell University, Professor Robert E. Lord of Harvard, Professor Charles Seymour of Yale, Hon. Henry Morgenthau, former ambassador to Turkey, Dir. Isaiah Bowman, director of the American Geographical Society, Professor Manley O. Hudson of Harvard and other men of world wide fame as were more or less prominently connected with the proceedings at the peace conference.

In addition to the public lectures the undergraduates, divided into selected groups, have had the opportunity to question these lecturers at round table conferences, where lecturers and students came into close comradeship in the discussion of problems of international importance. In addition there were two very interesting lectures, Professor Seymour speaking in the afternoon on "THE Adriatic Problem" and Professor Manley O. Hudson of Harvard in the evening on "THE United States and the World Politics of Today."

President Stills' Remarks
